Phylogenetic Generalized Linear Mixed Model for Community Data

Source: R/pglmm.R
pglmm.Rd

This function performs Generalized Linear Mixed Models for binary, count, and continuous data, estimating regression coefficients with approximate standard errors. It is specifically designed for community data in which species occur within multiple sites (locations). A Bayesian version of PGLMM uses the package INLA, which is not available on CRAN yet. If you wish to use this option, you must first install INLA from https://www.r-inla.org/ by running install.packages('INLA', repos='https://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/R/stable') in R.

Usage

pglmm(
  formula,
  data = NULL,
  family = "gaussian",
  cov_ranef = NULL,
  random.effects = NULL,
  REML = TRUE,
  optimizer = NULL,
  repulsion = FALSE,
  add.obs.re = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  cpp = TRUE,
  bayes = FALSE,
  s2.init = NULL,
  B.init = NULL,
  reltol = 10^-6,
  maxit = 500,
  tol.pql = 10^-6,
  maxit.pql = 200,
  marginal.summ = "mean",
  calc.DIC = TRUE,
  calc.WAIC = TRUE,
  prior = "inla.default",
  prior_alpha = 0.1,
  prior_mu = 1,
  ML.init = FALSE,
  tree = NULL,
  tree_site = NULL,
  sp = NULL,
  site = NULL,
  bayes_options = NULL,
  bayes_nested_matrix_as_list = FALSE,
  posterior.sample = TRUE,
  return.fitted.marginals = TRUE,
  sparse = NULL,
  standardize_cov = TRUE,
  method = c("Laplace", "PQL"),
  sparse_method = c("precision", "flow")
)

communityPGLMM(
  formula,
  data = NULL,
  family = "gaussian",
  cov_ranef = NULL,
  random.effects = NULL,
  REML = TRUE,
  optimizer = NULL,
  repulsion = FALSE,
  add.obs.re = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  cpp = TRUE,
  bayes = FALSE,
  s2.init = NULL,
  B.init = NULL,
  reltol = 10^-6,
  maxit = 500,
  tol.pql = 10^-6,
  maxit.pql = 200,
  marginal.summ = "mean",
  calc.DIC = TRUE,
  calc.WAIC = TRUE,
  prior = "inla.default",
  prior_alpha = 0.1,
  prior_mu = 1,
  ML.init = FALSE,
  tree = NULL,
  tree_site = NULL,
  sp = NULL,
  site = NULL,
  bayes_options = NULL,
  bayes_nested_matrix_as_list = FALSE,
  posterior.sample = TRUE,
  return.fitted.marginals = TRUE,
  sparse = NULL,
  standardize_cov = TRUE,
  method = c("Laplace", "PQL"),
  sparse_method = c("precision", "flow")
)

Arguments

formula

A two-sided linear formula object describing the mixed effects of the model.

To specify that a random term should have phylogenetic covariance matrix along with non-phylogenetic one, add __ (two underscores) at the end of the group variable; e.g., + (1 | sp__) will construct two random terms, one with phylogenetic covariance matrix and another with non-phylogenetic (identity) matrix. In contrast, __ in the nested terms (below) will only create a phylogenetic covariance matrix. Nested random terms have the general form (1|sp__@site__) which represents phylogenetically related species nested within correlated sites. This form can be used for bipartite questions. For example, species could be phylogenetically related pollinators and sites could be phylogenetically related plants, leading to the random effect (1|insects__@plants__). If more than one phylogeny is used, remember to add all to the argument cov_ranef = list(insects = insect_phylo, plants = plant_phylo). Phylogenetic correlations can be dropped by removing the __ underscores. Thus, the form (1|sp@site__) excludes the phylogenetic correlations among species, while the form (1|sp__@site) excludes the correlations among sites.

Note that correlated random terms are not allowed. For example, (x|g) will be the same as (0 + x|g) in the lme4::lmer syntax. However, (x1 + x2|g) won't work, so instead use (x1|g) + (x2|g), or (x1 + x2||g). As the random intercept and slope of (1|g) + (x|g) are independent, the model depends on where x is zero: the variance among the levels of g is that of the intercept plus \(x^2\) times that of the slope. With a 0/1 covariate (e.g. a control and a treatment), the levels then vary more in the treatment than in the control by construction. Center continuous covariates of random slopes (e.g. x - mean(x)) and code two-level factors as -1/+1 (equal variance in both groups) unless zero is a meaningful reference. Covariates of random slopes must be numeric columns of data.

Grouping factors are columns of data. Their interactions as in lme4, e.g. (1|sp:site), are fitted as the nested terms (1|sp@site), and (1|site/sp) as (1|site) + (1|sp@site).

The formula can have offsets, e.g. + offset(log(effort)) for counts with different sampling efforts or areas: terms of the linear predictor with a known coefficient of one. They are supported with method = "Laplace" (binomial, poisson and negative binomial models) and bayes = TRUE, and are included in the predicted values (predict(), fitted(), simulate(); with newdata, the offset is calculated from it).

data

A data.frame containing the variables named in formula. Rows with missing values in the response, the fixed effects, the grouping variables or the covariates of random slopes are dropped before fitting; this is equivalent to removing those rows from data manually before calling pglmm. As a result, pglmm(data_with_NAs) and pglmm(na.omit(data[, vars])) (with vars the variables of the model) produce identical estimates. With random.effects, only the rows with missing values in the response are dropped.

family

Either "gaussian" for a Linear Mixed Model, or "binomial", "poisson", "nbinomial" or "Gamma" for Generalized Linear Mixed Models. "family" should be specified as a character string (i.e., quoted). For binomial and Poisson data, we use the canonical logit and log link functions, respectively. Binomial data can be either presence/absence, or a two-column array of 'successes' and 'failures'. For both binomial and Poisson data, we add an observation-level random term by default via add.obs.re = TRUE.

"nbinomial" is the negative binomial distribution for overdispersed counts, with the log link and the variance \(\mu + \mu^2 / \theta\) given the random effects (as lme4::glmer.nb(), glmmTMB(family = nbinom2) and MASS::glm.nb()). Its dispersion parameter \(\theta\) is estimated with the other parameters (element theta of the fitted model); \(\theta = \infty\) is the poisson distribution. As \(\theta\) accounts for overdispersion, no observation-level random term is added. With bayes = FALSE, negative binomial models are always fitted with method = "Laplace", with starting values from MASS::glm.nb().

"Gamma" (or "gamma") is the Gamma distribution for positive continuous responses (e.g. biomass, body size, durations), with the log link and the variance \(\mu^2 / \nu\) given the random effects (as glm(), lme4::glmer() and glmmTMB() with family = Gamma(link = "log")). Its shape parameter \(\nu\) is estimated with the other parameters (element shape of the fitted model; sigma() of glmmTMB is \(1/\sqrt{\nu}\), the coefficient of variation). No observation-level random term is added. Gamma models are only available with bayes = FALSE, and are always fitted with method = "Laplace", with starting values from glm() and MASS::gamma.shape().

If bayes = TRUE there are three additional families available: "zeroinflated.binomial", "zeroinflated.poisson" and "zeroinflated.nbinomial", which add a zero inflation parameter; this parameter gives the probability that the response is a zero. The rest of the parameters of the model then reflect the "non-zero" part part of the model. Note that "zeroinflated.binomial" only makes sense for success/failure response data.

cov_ranef

A named list of covariance matrices of random terms. The names should be the group variables that are used as random terms with specified covariance matrices (without the two underscores, e.g. list(sp = tree1, site = tree2)). The actual object can be either a phylogeny with class "phylo" or a prepared covariance matrix. If it is a phylogeny, pglmm will prune it and then convert it to a covariance matrix assuming Brownian motion evolution. pglmm will also standardize all covariance matrices to have determinant of one (unless standardize_cov = FALSE), so the estimated variances of these terms are on the scale of the standardized matrices; use scale_factors of the fitted model to rescale them (see "Extracting the variances of random terms" in Details). Group variables will be converted to factors and all covariance matrices will be rearranged so that rows and columns are in the same order as the levels of their corresponding group variables.

random.effects

Optional pre-build list of random effects. If NULL (the default), the function prep_dat_pglmm will prepare the random effects for you from the information in formula, data, and cov_ranef. random.effect allows a list of pre-generated random effects terms to increase flexibility; for example, this makes it possible to construct models with both phylogenetic correlation and spatio-temporal autocorrelation. In preparing random.effect, make sure that the orders of rows and columns of covariance matrices in the list are the same as their corresponding group variables in the data. Also, this should be a list of lists, e.g. random.effects = list(re1 = list(matrix_a), re2 = list(1, sp = sp, covar = Vsp)).

REML

Whether REML or ML is used for model fitting the random effects. Ignored if bayes = TRUE. For binomial and poisson models with method = "Laplace", REML = TRUE integrates the fixed effects out of the likelihood with the Laplace approximation too (as glmmTMB(REML = TRUE)); use REML = FALSE for maximum likelihood estimates, comparable with lme4::glmer() and glmmTMB().

optimizer

Optimizer to use. Options: "lbfgs" (L-BFGS with analytic gradient; default for Gaussian, also available for binomial/Poisson), "nelder-mead-nlopt" (default for binomial/Poisson), "bobyqa", "Nelder-Mead", or "subplex". "Nelder-Mead" is from the stats package; all others are from the nloptr package. With sparse = TRUE, the default (and "lbfgs") is nlminb() with the analytic gradient of the likelihood (see sparse); "subplex", "nelder-mead-nlopt", "Nelder-Mead" (both the Nelder-Mead algorithm of nloptr) and "bobyqa" are derivative-free, and the optimizer is restarted from its solution until the likelihood does not improve (for gaussian models; for binomial and poisson models, each PQL iteration already starts the optimizer from the previous solution). Ignored if bayes = TRUE or method = "Laplace".

repulsion

When there are nested random terms specified, repulsion = FALSE tests for phylogenetic underdispersion while repulsion = TRUE tests for overdispersion. This argument is a logical vector of length either 1 or >1. If its length is 1, it applies to the phylogenies of species only (the variable before @, e.g. sp in sp__@site and sp__@site__): their covariance matrices are either inverted (overdispersion) or not, while the phylogenies of sites (after @) are never inverted. This follows Ives and Helmus (2011, Appendix A), where repulsion arises from competition among closely related species. If it has more than one element, then you can select which covariance matrix in the nested terms to be inverted. Make sure to get the length right: for all the terms with @, count the number of "__" to determine the length of repulsion. For example, sp__@site and sp@site__ will each require one element of repulsion, while sp__@site__ will take two elements (repulsion for sp and repulsion for site). Therefore, if your nested terms are (1|sp__@site) + (1|sp@site__) + (1|sp__@site__), then you should set the repulsion to be something like c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE) (length of 4).

add.obs.re

Whether to add an observation-level random term for binomial or Poisson distributions. Normally it would be a good idea to add this to account for overdispersion, so add.obs.re = TRUE by default.

verbose

If TRUE, the model deviance and running estimates of s2 and B are plotted each iteration during optimization.

cpp

Whether to use C++ function for optim. Default is TRUE. Only used by the dense code (sparse = FALSE, which is the default only for models that the sparse code does not support, see sparse); ignored if bayes = TRUE, sparse = TRUE or method = "Laplace" (and thus for family = "nbinomial" and "Gamma"): these models are fitted with R code, with the sparse Cholesky factorizations of the Matrix package (CHOLMOD).

bayes

Whether to fit a Bayesian version of the PGLMM using r-inla.

s2.init

An array of initial estimates of s2 for each random effect that scales the variance. If s2.init is not provided for family="gaussian", these are estimated using lm assuming no phylogenetic signal. A better approach might be to run link[lme4:lmer]{lmer} and use the output random effects for s2.init. If s2.init is not provided for family = "binomial", these are set to 0.25 (with method = "Laplace", 0.25 for the variances multiplied by scale_factors). For family = "gaussian" and bayes = FALSE, the model is parameterized with the variances of random terms relative to the residual variance (see ss in the Value section), and s2.init gives the starting values of these ratios.

B.init

Initial estimates of \(B\), a matrix containing regression coefficients in the model for the fixed effects. This matrix must have dim(B.init) = c(p + 1, 1), where p is the number of predictor (independent) variables; the first element of B corresponds to the intercept, and the remaining elements correspond in order to the predictor (independent) variables in the formula. If B.init is not provided, these are estimated using lm or glm assuming no phylogenetic signal. A better approach might be to run lmer and use the output fixed effects for B.init. When bayes = TRUE, initial values are estimated using the maximum likelihood fit unless ML.init = FALSE, in which case the default INLA initial values will be used.

reltol

A control parameter dictating the relative tolerance for convergence in the optimization; see optim. With sparse = TRUE, the default is 1e-8 (for each run of the optimizer, including each PQL iteration of binomial and poisson models). With method = "Laplace", the relative tolerance of nlminb() (default 1e-10); maxit is then its maximum number of iterations and evaluations.

maxit

A control parameter dictating the maximum number of iterations in the optimization; see optim.

tol.pql

A control parameter dictating the tolerance for convergence in the PQL estimates of the mean components of the GLMM. Ignored if family = "gaussian", bayes = TRUE, or method = "Laplace".

maxit.pql

A control parameter dictating the maximum number of iterations in the PQL estimates of the mean components of the GLMM. Ignored if family = "gaussian" or bayes = TRUE.

marginal.summ

Summary statistic to use for the estimate of coefficients when doing a Bayesian PGLMM (when bayes = TRUE). Options are: "mean", "median", or "mode", referring to different characterizations of the central tendency of the Bayesian posterior marginal distributions. Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

calc.DIC

Should the Deviance Information Criterion be calculated and returned when doing a Bayesian PGLMM? Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

calc.WAIC

Should the WAIC be calculated and returned when doing a Bayesian PGLMM? Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

prior

Which type of default prior should be used by pglmm? Only used if bayes = TRUE. There are currently four options: "inla.default", which uses the default INLA priors; "pc.prior.auto", which uses a complexity penalizing prior (as described in Simpson et al. (2017)) designed to automatically choose good parameters (only available for gaussian and binomial responses); "pc.prior", which allows the user to set custom parameters on the "pc.prior" prior, using the prior_alpha and prior_mu parameters (Run INLA::inla.doc("pc.prec") for details on these parameters); and "uninformative", which sets a very uninformative prior (nearly uniform) by using a very flat exponential distribution. The last option is generally not recommended but may in some cases give estimates closer to the maximum likelihood estimates. "pc.prior.auto" is only implemented for family = "gaussian" and family = "binomial" currently.

prior_alpha

Only used if bayes = TRUE and prior = "pc.prior", in which case it sets the alpha parameter of INLA's complexity penalizing prior for the random effects. The prior is an exponential distribution where prob(sd > mu) = alpha, where sd is the standard deviation of the random effect.

prior_mu

Only used if bayes = TRUE and prior = "pc.prior", in which case it sets the mu parameter of INLA's complexity penalizing prior for the random effects. The prior is an exponential distribution where prob(sd > mu) = alpha, where sd is the standard deviation of the random effect.

ML.init

Only relevant if bayes = TRUE. Should maximum likelihood estimates be calculated and used as initial values for the Bayesian model fit? Sometimes this can be helpful, but it may not help; thus, we set the default to FALSE. Also, it does not work with the zero-inflated families.

tree

A phylogeny for column sp, with "phylo" class, or a covariance matrix for sp. Make sure to have all species in the matrix; if the matrix is not standardized, (i.e., det(tree) != 1), pglmm will try to standardize it for you. No longer used: keep here for compatibility.

tree_site

A second phylogeny for "site". This is required only if the site column contains species instead of sites. This can be used for bipartitie questions; tree_site can also be a covariance matrix. Make sure to have all sites in the matrix; if the matrix is not standardized (i.e., det(tree_site) != 1), pglmm` will try to standardize it for you. No longer used: keep here for compatibility.

sp

No longer used: keep here for compatibility.

site

No longer used: keep here for compatibility.

bayes_options

Additional options to pass to INLA when bayes = TRUE. A named list where the names correspond to parameters in the inla function. One special option is diagonal: if an element in the list is named diagonal, INLA adds its value to the diagonal of every random-effects precision matrix, which can help with numerical stability when the model is ill-conditioned (try list(diagonal = 1e-4) if you see many warnings). To use multiple CPU cores, pass list(num.threads = 4) (or however many cores are available); this is often the single most effective way to speed up INLA. Any control.compute entries supplied here override the defaults set by posterior.sample and return.fitted.marginals.

bayes_nested_matrix_as_list

For bayes = TRUE, prepare the nested terms as a list of length 4 as the old way?

posterior.sample

Logical (default TRUE). Only used when bayes = TRUE. When TRUE, INLA stores the full joint posterior configuration (control.compute = list(config = TRUE)), which is required for simulate to work. Set to FALSE to skip this storage and speed up fitting when posterior simulation is not needed.

return.fitted.marginals

Logical (default TRUE). Only used when bayes = TRUE. When TRUE, INLA computes and returns the marginal posterior distributions of all fitted values (control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE)), which is required for simulate with full = FALSE. Set to FALSE to skip this computation and speed up fitting when simulation is not needed. If both posterior.sample and return.fitted.marginals are FALSE, INLA runs at maximum speed but simulate() will not work on the fitted model.

sparse

Whether to fit the model with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (TRUE) or with the dense covariance matrices (FALSE). The default, NULL, is TRUE whenever the sparse code supports the model, i.e. with random terms in the formula (not random.effects), phylogenies (class phylo, not covariance matrices) in cov_ranef, and, with bayes = TRUE, ML.init = FALSE and repulsion = FALSE; FALSE otherwise (it was FALSE before phyr 1.5.0). Both give the same model; the estimates can differ slightly, as the optimizers differ (for binomial and poisson models fitted by PQL, the log-likelihood also depends on the path of the iterations). With TRUE, the model is fitted with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (which includes its internal nodes) and a sparse Cholesky decomposition, instead of the dense phylogenetic covariance matrix. This gives the same likelihood, but the time and memory needed grow about linearly with the number of species, so that models with thousands of species can be fitted. Nested terms (e.g. (1 | sp__@site), (1 | sp@site__), (1 | sp__@site__), (1 | sp@site)) use the precision matrix of the Kronecker product of the two covariance matrices; their time grows about linearly with the number of species and somewhat faster than linearly with the number of sites. With repulsion = TRUE, the precision matrix of the phylogeny becomes its (dense) covariance matrix, which is written with the internal nodes as auxiliary variables, and a sparse \(LDL'\) decomposition of a larger (indefinite) matrix is used instead. Binomial and poisson models are fitted with the same penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL) iterations as with sparse = FALSE (same updates and convergence rules, tol.pql and maxit.pql); at each iteration, the working weights change only the values of the sparse matrix, and the observation-level term 1|obs is folded into the weights. Only available with phylogenies (class phylo) in cov_ranef. With bayes = TRUE, the model is given to INLA with one of the sparse representations of sparse_method; use sparse = FALSE for the dense INLA model of earlier versions (needed for ranef(), predict() with newdata and simulate() with re.form = NA, see sparse_method).

With bayes = FALSE, the variances (for gaussian models, relative to the residual variance; for binomial and poisson models, at each PQL iteration) are estimated with nlminb() and the analytic gradient of the likelihood, with a relative tolerance reltol = 1e-10 by default. The gradient needs the entries of the inverse of the sparse matrix on its pattern (its selected inverse, from the Cholesky factor, in C++), which cost about as much as a factorization. As for method = "Laplace", the variances are optimized multiplied by their scale_factors, with a lower bound of zero (in practice \(10^{-12}\), reported as zero). As a phylogenetic term such as 1|sp__ and its non-phylogenetic partner 1|sp are nearly confounded, the likelihood can have a local optimum where both variances are positive, and a better one where one of them is zero; the optimization is thus also started from the two "corners" where one of these variances has their sum and the other is zero, and the best solution is kept (each corner is first tried with a few iterations, and the optimization goes on only if it is then already better). The derivative-free optimizers of earlier versions can still be used with optimizer = "subplex", "nelder-mead-nlopt" or "bobyqa" (with reltol = 1e-8 by default); "lbfgs" also uses nlminb() and the gradient. ranef(condVar = TRUE) uses the selected inverse too.

The sparse precision matrix exists because the trait evolves along the branches as a Markov process (the value at a node depends only on its parent). This is not limited to Brownian motion: any model that is Brownian motion on a tree with transformed branch lengths can be used by passing the transformed phylogeny in cov_ranef, e.g. an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model with a fixed \(\alpha\) (phylolm::transf.branch.lengths(tree, model = "OUfixedRoot", parameters = list(alpha = a))$tree or geiger::rescale(tree, "OU", alpha = a)), Pagel's \(\lambda\), \(\kappa\), or \(\delta\), or early burst. As with sparse = FALSE, the parameters of these models (e.g. \(\alpha\)) are not estimated by pglmm(); they can be chosen by fitting the model over a grid of values and comparing the log-likelihoods, which is fast with sparse = TRUE. With standardize_cov = TRUE, the overall scale of the transformed tree (e.g. \(\sigma^2\) of the OU model) has no effect. The OU transformation is exact for ultrametric trees; for non-ultrametric trees, check that it matches the assumption about the root. Covariance matrices that cannot be written as a tree with non-negative branch lengths (e.g. an arbitrary similarity matrix) need sparse = FALSE.

standardize_cov

Logical (default TRUE). Whether to standardize the covariance matrices of cov_ranef to have a determinant of one (a phylogeny is first converted to its covariance matrix, which is divided by its largest element). If FALSE, the matrices are used as given: a covariance matrix is used as it is, and a phylogeny gives ape::vcv(tree), on the scale of its branch lengths. The variances of the random terms (s2r, s2n) are then on the scale of these matrices, so that, e.g., the variance of 1|sp__ with a phylogenetic correlation matrix (ape::vcv(tree, corr = TRUE)) or an ultrametric tree with a height of one is directly comparable with the variance of 1|sp and with software that does not standardize the matrices. The likelihood, the fixed effects and the predictions do not depend on this choice; only the scale of the variances (and of s2.init) does. Not used when random.effects is given.

method

For binomial and poisson models with bayes = FALSE, the approximation of the likelihood (negative binomial and Gamma models, family = "nbinomial" and "Gamma", are always fitted with "Laplace"): "Laplace" (default since phyr 1.5.0) for the Laplace approximation of the marginal likelihood, as in lme4::glmer() (with nAGQ = 1) and glmmTMB, or "PQL" for penalized quasi-likelihood (the default of earlier versions, and with random.effects, which the Laplace code does not support). PQL is known to underestimate the variances of random terms, and to shrink the fixed effects towards zero, for binary data and counts with small means; the Laplace approximation is much less biased, and its log-likelihood approximates the marginal likelihood of the model, so that it can be used for likelihood ratio tests (pglmm_profile_LRT()) and AIC (the log-likelihood of PQL is that of a gaussian model of the working response). Ignored for gaussian models (their likelihood is exact) and with bayes = TRUE.

With "Laplace", the model is always fitted with the precision matrices used by sparse = TRUE, whatever the value of sparse: a phylogeny gives the sparse precision matrix of all its nodes, and a covariance matrix in cov_ranef its (dense) inverse. The time to fit a model thus grows about linearly with the number of species, and nested terms and repulsion are supported. The random terms must be given in the formula (random.effects is not supported: models with it are fitted with PQL by default). The mode of the random effects (including the observation-level term 1|obs) is found by Newton iterations. The variances of the random terms are estimated first with the fixed effects at the mode (as glmer(nAGQ = 0)); this is the final fit with REML = TRUE, where the fixed effects are integrated out (as glmmTMB(REML = TRUE)) and their covariance matrix is conditional on the variances. With REML = FALSE, the fixed effects and the variances are then estimated jointly (as glmer(nAGQ = 1) and glmmTMB), and the covariance matrix of the fixed effects is from the inverse of the (numerical) Hessian of the log-likelihood over the fixed effects and the standard deviations of the random terms, as in these packages. The optimizer is nlminb(), on the scale of the variances multiplied by their scale_factors (the variances of an average level, with a lower bound of zero; the default starting values are 0.25 on this scale), and of the dispersion of negative binomial and Gamma models (\(1/\theta\), 1/shape), with analytic gradients, restarted from the corners of the variances of phylogenetic terms and their partners (see sparse); optimizer, tol.pql and maxit.pql are not used. ranef() gives the conditional modes of the random effects, and condVar = TRUE their conditional standard deviations from the Hessian of the Laplace approximation (conditional on the estimates of the parameters). pglmm_iV() gives the inverse of the covariance matrix of the working response at the mode.

Choosing between them:

  • "PQL" (the default of earlier versions): often faster (about 1–3 times with sparse = TRUE), supports every model of pglmm() (including random.effects), and gives the same estimates as earlier versions of phyr. But its estimates are biased for binary data: compared with "Laplace" (and glmer()/glmmTMB), the fixed effects were about 5–10% closer to zero and the variances of random terms about 10–30% smaller in our comparisons. For counts, the differences were small (variances a few percent smaller). Its log-likelihood is not that of the model, so AIC and likelihood ratio tests (including tests for phylogenetic signal with pglmm_profile_LRT()) are only rough approximations.

  • "Laplace" (default): gives the same estimates and log-likelihood as lme4::glmer() and glmmTMB (to optimizer tolerance), much less biased estimates (about unbiased fixed effects with REML = FALSE, and the least biased phylogenetic variance with REML = TRUE), and a log-likelihood that can be used for AIC and likelihood ratio tests. Still much faster than glmmTMB for large phylogenies (e.g. 1 s versus about 60 s for 2000 species). Use it when the variances of random terms, tests of phylogenetic signal, or model comparisons matter, especially for binary data. It is an approximation too: for binary data with few observations per species, the variances (especially the phylogenetic one) remain underestimated with REML = FALSE, as with any maximum likelihood fit; REML = TRUE reduces this bias.

sparse_method

With sparse = TRUE and bayes = TRUE, how the phylogenetic terms are given to INLA. "precision" (default): as a latent field over all nodes of the phylogeny (tips and internal nodes, without the root), with the sparse precision matrix of sparse = TRUE; the posterior of the internal nodes (ancestral states) comes with the fit. "flow": in the phylogenetic flow representation of the phyf and fibre packages, as independent rates of evolution \(r_b\) on the branches, \(u_i = \sum_b \ell_b r_b\) for the branches \(b\) from the root to tip \(i\), with \(r_b \sim N(0, \sigma^2 / \ell_b)\) and \(\ell_b\) the (standardized) branch lengths. The trait then changes by \(\ell_b r_b\) along each branch, with variance \(\sigma^2 \ell_b\), so that the covariance matrix of the tips is the same as with "precision" (Brownian motion), and the two give the same model; "flow" gives the posterior of the rates, on the scale of the trait per unit of branch length of the phylogenies in cov_ranef. For nested terms with phylogenies (e.g. (1 | sp__@site), (1 | sp__@site__)), the rates are those of the pairs of branches (or of a branch and a level), from the row-wise Kronecker product of the two flow matrices, with \(r \sim N(0, \sigma^2 / (\ell_1 \ell_2))\), which gives the covariance matrix of the Kronecker product of the two covariance matrices. Terms without phylogeny are the same with both methods. The estimates of the rates ("flow") or of the nodes of non-nested phylogenetic terms ("precision") are in bayes_sparse$latent of the fitted model. Both methods report the marginal log-likelihood of the model (logLik; with "flow", INLA's value with the matrix A can differ from that of "precision" by about one unit); "flow" is only available with bayes = TRUE for now. repulsion, ML.init, ranef(), predict() with newdata and simulate() with re.form = NA (any simulate() for "flow") are not available yet for these models. With "flow", the rates are linked to the observations by the matrix A of control.predictor of INLA (as in fibre), so inla.model has more fitted values than observations (the first ones are those of the observations).

Value

An object (list) of class communityPGLMM with the following elements:

formula

the formula for fixed effects

formula_original

the formula for both fixed effects and random effects

call

the call of pglmm(), used by update() (and anova(), to refit REML fits by maximum likelihood)

re_terms

the random terms of the formula, as a named list (one element per term, e.g. "1|sp" and "1|sp__" for (1 | sp__)) with the covariate (lhs, "1" for intercepts), the grouping variables (group), whether each has a phylogeny or covariance matrix (phy), and whether the term is nested (nested) and, for nested terms, whether each covariance matrix is inverted (repulsion); NULL with random.effects

data

the dataset

family

gaussian, binomial, poisson, nbinomial or Gamma depending on the model fit

theta

for negative binomial models, the estimate of the dispersion parameter \(\theta\) (Inf if the data are not overdispersed: the poisson model); for bayes = TRUE, its posterior summary, with the credible interval in theta.ci. It is sigma() of glmmTMB(family = nbinom2) models and getME(, "glmer.nb.theta") of lme4::glmer.nb() models.

shape

for Gamma models, the estimate of the shape parameter \(\nu\) (the variance is \(\mu^2 / \nu\)); 1 / sigma()^2 of glmmTMB() models with family = Gamma(link = "log").

random.effects

the list of random effects

B

estimates of the regression coefficients

B.se

approximate standard errors of the fixed effects regression coefficients. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE.

B.ci

approximate Bayesian credible interval of the fixed effects regression coefficients. This is set to NULL if bayes = FALSE

B.cov

approximate covariance matrix for the fixed effects regression coefficients

B.zscore

approximate Z scores for the fixed effects regression coefficients. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

B.pvalue

approximate tests for the fixed effects regression coefficients being different from zero. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

ss

the parameters that are optimized when fitting the model, one for each random term (non-nested terms first, then nested terms). Their meaning depends on the model:

  • For gaussian models with bayes = FALSE, they are the standard deviations of the random terms relative to the residual standard deviation, i.e. \(\sigma_i / \sigma_{resid}\); the residual standard deviation itself is listed last. The residual variance is profiled out of the likelihood, so only these ratios are optimized (this is the same parameterization as theta of lme4 for a term such as (1 | g)). The variances are s2r = s2resid * ss^2 and s2n = s2resid * ss^2 for the corresponding elements.

  • For binomial and poisson models with bayes = FALSE, and for all models with bayes = TRUE, they are the standard deviations \(\sigma_i\) of the random terms themselves (ss^2 equals s2r and s2n); for gaussian models with bayes = TRUE the residual standard deviation is listed last.

In all cases, the covariance contribution of the ith term is \(\sigma_i^2 V_{i,\rm std}\), where \(V_{i,\rm std}\) is the det=1 standardized covariance matrix (see Details), so these are not standard deviations on the original covariance scale. For variance inference use s2r, s2n, or s2resid (or VarCorr()); do not use ss^2 as a variance estimate for gaussian models.

s2r

variance parameters \(\sigma_i^2\) for non-nested random effects, relative to the det=1 standardized covariance matrices (see Details). These are the recommended output for variance inference. To obtain the effective per-observation variance on a scale comparable across all random effects (including non-phylogenetic terms), multiply by scale_factors: s2r * scale_factors[names(s2r)].

s2n

variance parameters for nested random effects; same scale as s2r. Use s2n * scale_factors[names(s2n)] for the comparable per-observation variance.

s2resid

for linear mixed models, the residual variance. The residual always uses an identity covariance matrix (scale_factor = 1), so s2resid is directly interpretable without any rescaling.

scale_factors

named numeric vector with one entry per random effect term. Each value is mean(diag(V_std)), the mean diagonal of the det=1 standardized covariance matrix for that term (averaged over its levels, not over observations); with standardize_cov = FALSE, the mean diagonal of the matrix as given. For identity-based (non-phylogenetic) terms this equals 1, meaning s2r is already on an interpretable scale. For a phylogenetic term from an ultrametric tree or a correlation matrix, this equals \(1 / \det(V_{\rm orig})^{1/n}\) and is typically much larger than 1. Multiplying s2r[i] * scale_factors[i] gives the variance of the ith random effect for an average level, comparable across all terms in the model and with software that does not standardize the covariance matrices (see Details).

s2r.ci

Bayesian credible interval for random effects variances for non-nested random effects. This is set to NULL if bayes = FALSE

s2n.ci

Bayesian credible interval for random effects variances for nested random effects. This is set to NULL if bayes = FALSE

s2resid.ci

Bayesian credible interval for linear mixed models, the residual variance. This is set to NULL if bayes = FALSE

logLik

the log-likelihood, restricted (REML = TRUE) or not (REML = FALSE). For gaussian models with REML = TRUE, it is the restricted log-likelihood of lmer(), glmmTMB() and nlme::lme() (the likelihood integrated over the fixed effects); versions of phyr before 1.5.0 added \(\log|X'X|/2\) to it. For binomial and poisson models fitted with method = "PQL", it is an approximation from the gaussian model of the working response; with method = "Laplace", it is the Laplace approximation of the (restricted) marginal log-likelihood, the same as that of glmer() and glmmTMB(). If bayes = TRUE, this is the marginal log-likelihood of INLA

AIC

the AIC calculated with logLik (bayes = FALSE)

BIC

the BIC calculated with logLik (bayes = FALSE)

method

for binomial and poisson models with bayes = FALSE, the approximation of the likelihood, "PQL" or "Laplace" (see the argument method)

DIC

for Bayesian PGLMM, this is the Deviance Information Criterion metric of model fit. This is set to NULL if bayes = FALSE.

REML

whether or not REML is used (TRUE or FALSE).

bayes

whether or not a Bayesian model was fit.

standardize_cov

the value of the argument standardize_cov.

marginal.summ

The specified summary statistic used to summarize the Bayesian marginal distributions. Only present if bayes = TRUE

s2.init

the user-provided initial estimates of s2

B.init

the user-provided initial estimates of B

Y

the response (dependent) variable returned in matrix form

size

the number of trials of each observation for binomial models (it is one for binary data, and for poisson models). This is NULL for gaussian models, and for models with bayes = TRUE unless the response is specified with the numbers of successes and failures.

X

the predictor (independent) variables returned in matrix form (including 1s in the first column)

H

the residuals. For linear mixed models, this does not account for random terms, i.e. it is similar to Y - predict(merMod, re.form = NA) for models fitted with lme4. To get residuals after accounting for both fixed and random terms, use residuals(). For the generalized linear mixed model, these are the predicted residuals in the logit -1 space.

mu

predicted mean values for the generalized linear mixed model (i.e., similar to fitted(merMod)). Set to NULL for linear mixed models, for which we can use fitted().

nested

matrices used to construct the nested design matrix. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

Zt

the design matrix for random effects. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

St

diagonal matrix that maps the random effects variances onto the design matrix

convcode

the convergence code provided by optim. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

niter

number of iterations performed by optim. This is set to NULL if bayes = TRUE

inla.model

Model object fit by underlying inla function. Only returned if bayes = TRUE

Details

For Gaussian data, pglmm analyzes the phylogenetic linear mixed model

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + b_0 + b_1x$$ $$b_0 ~ Gaussian(0, \sigma_0^2I_{sp})$$ $$b_1 ~ Gaussian(0, \sigma_0^2V_{sp})$$ $$\eta ~ Gaussian(0,\sigma^2)$$

where \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are fixed effects, and \(V_{sp}\) is a variance-covariance matrix derived from a phylogeny (typically under the assumption of Brownian motion evolution). Here, the variation in the mean (intercept) for each species is given by the random effect \(b_0\) that is assumed to be independent among species. Variation in species' responses to predictor variable \(x\) is given by a random effect \(b_0\) that is assumed to depend on the phylogenetic relatedness among species given by \(V_{sp}\); if species are closely related, their specific responses to \(x\) will be similar. This particular model would be specified as

z <- pglmm(Y ~ X + (1|sp__), data = data, family = "gaussian", cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))

Or you can prepare the random terms manually (not recommended for simple models but may be necessary for complex models):

re.1 <- list(1, sp = dat$sp, covar = diag(nspp))

re.2 <- list(dat$X, sp = dat$sp, covar = Vsp)

z <- pglmm(Y ~ X, data = data, family = "gaussian", random.effects = list(re.1, re.2))

By default (standardize_cov = TRUE), the covariance matrix \(V\) is standardized to have determinant equal to 1 before fitting. Specifically, for an \(n \times n\) covariance matrix \(V\), pglmm uses \(V_{\rm std} = V / \det(V)^{1/n}\), which has \(\det(V_{\rm std}) = 1\). This ensures that the variance parameter \(\sigma^2\) has a consistent scale regardless of the absolute magnitude of \(V\).

Extracting the variances of random terms. Two things are easy to get wrong when the estimated variances are reported, or compared with those of other software (e.g. glmmTMB, MCMCglmm, brms) or with the values used to simulate data:

  1. Use s2r, s2n and s2resid (or VarCorr()), not ss^2. For gaussian models fitted with bayes = FALSE, ss holds the standard deviations of the random terms relative to the residual standard deviation (s2r = s2resid * ss^2), so ss^2 is not a variance; it is too large by a factor of 1 / s2resid (see ss in Value).

  2. The variance of a term with a covariance matrix is on the scale of the standardized matrix. The model is fitted as \(\sigma^2 V_{\rm std}\), so s2r and s2n are relative to \(V_{\rm std}\), not to the matrix (or phylogeny) given in cov_ranef. Standardizing a phylogenetic correlation matrix (diagonal of 1) to a determinant of one inflates its diagonal (often several-fold, more with more species), whereas the identity matrix of a non-phylogenetic term such as 1|sp is unchanged. As a result, the s2r of 1|sp and 1|sp__ are not on the same scale, and the s2r of 1|sp__ is much smaller than the phylogenetic variance on the scale of the correlation matrix. To put a term on the scale of an average level (for a correlation matrix or an ultrametric tree, the scale of the original matrix), multiply it by the mean diagonal of the standardized matrix: $$\sigma^2_{\rm obs} = \sigma^2_{\rm std} \times \overline{\rm diag}(V_{\rm std})$$ The fitted model returns these factors as scale_factors (1 for terms without a covariance matrix and for the residual): fit$s2r * fit$scale_factors[names(fit$s2r)] and fit$s2n * fit$scale_factors[names(fit$s2n)]. Do this before comparing the variances of different terms (e.g. to calculate the proportion of the variance among species that is phylogenetic) or comparing them with other software. Alternatively, fit the model with standardize_cov = FALSE, so that the variances are on the scale of the matrices as given (with a phylogeny, on the scale of its branch lengths).

The estimates of fixed effects, the likelihood, and the group-level estimates of ranef() do not depend on the standardization.

Although mathematically this is not required, it is a very good idea to standardize the predictor (independent) variables to have mean 0 and variance 1. This will make the function more robust and improve the interpretation of the regression coefficients. For categorical (factor) predictor variables, you will need to construct 0-1 dummy variables, and these should not be standardized (for obvious reasons).

For binary generalized linear mixed models (family = 'binomial'), the function estimates parameters for the model of the form, for example,

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + b_0 + b_1x$$ $$Y = logit^{-1}(y)$$ $$b_0 ~ Gaussian(0, \sigma_0^2I_{sp})$$ $$b_1 ~ Gaussian(0, \sigma_0^2V_{sp})$$

where \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are fixed effects, and \(V_{sp}\) is a variance-covariance matrix derived from a phylogeny (typically under the assumption of Brownian motion evolution).

z <- pglmm(Y ~ X + (1|sp__), data = data, family = "binomial", cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))

As with the linear mixed model, it is a very good idea to standardize the predictor (independent) variables to have mean 0 and variance 1. This will make the function more robust and improve the interpretation of the regression coefficients.

Speed

Models with bayes = FALSE spend most of their time in linear algebra (BLAS and LAPACK), so the BLAS library that R uses matters a lot for large data sets. The reference BLAS that R uses by default on some systems is much slower than optimized ones. On a Mac, R comes with a version that uses Apple's Accelerate; R can be switched to it by running, in a terminal, ln -sf libRblas.vecLib.dylib libRblas.dylib in the folder given by R.home("lib"), and restarting R (see the section about BLAS in the manual 'R Installation and Administration'). pglmm() shows a message once per session when a model with at least 1000 observations is fitted on a Mac with the reference BLAS; use options(phyr.blas.hint = FALSE) to turn it off. extSoftVersion()["BLAS"] shows the BLAS library that R uses.

For large models with a phylogeny (at least 2000 observations or 300 tips) fitted with sparse = FALSE, pglmm() shows a message once per session suggesting sparse = TRUE; use options(phyr.sparse.hint = FALSE) to turn it off.

Phylogenetic and non-phylogenetic terms

A phylogenetic term such as (1 | sp__) fits two terms, 1|sp__, with the phylogenetic covariance matrix, and 1|sp, independent among species; a random slope (x | sp__) likewise fits x|sp__ and x|sp. The variation among species is thus split between a part that follows the phylogeny (Brownian motion) and a part specific to each species (e.g. local adaptation, plasticity or measurement differences), and the data decide which is more important: either variance can be estimated as zero. Fitting the phylogenetic term alone (as with a single propto() term in glmmTMB) assumes that all the differences among species follow the phylogeny: the species-specific variation is then forced into the phylogenetic variance (or the residuals), which can distort it and the standard errors of the fixed effects. The ratio of the phylogenetic variance (multiplied by its scale_factors) to the sum of the two is a measure of phylogenetic signal, as Pagel's lambda (see the examples of VarCorr()).

The two terms are nearly confounded, and with few species or few rows per species, the data may not separate them well, even when their sum is well estimated. confint() gives profile likelihood intervals of the two variances, which are then both wide, and pglmm_profile_LRT() tests whether a term is needed (its p-value is halved, as a variance of zero is at the boundary of its range). The likelihood can also have a local optimum with both variances positive and a better one with one of them at zero, which the default optimizer of sparse = TRUE and method = "Laplace" checks (see sparse). The one case where the non-phylogenetic term cannot be estimated is comparative data, with one row per species (next section).

Comparative data

A phylogenetic term such as (1 | sp__) also adds the non-phylogenetic term (1 | sp). With comparative data (one row per species), that term is confounded with the residual variance (or with the observation-level term 1|obs); use pglmm_compare(), which fits the model with the phylogenetic term only. pglmm() shows a message once per session when each level of the grouping variable of a (non-nested) phylogenetic term has only one row; use options(phyr.compare.hint = FALSE) to turn it off.

References

Ives, A. R. and M. R. Helmus. 2011. Generalized linear mixed models for phylogenetic analyses of community structure. Ecological Monographs 81:511-525.

Ives A. R. 2018. Mixed and phylogenetic models: a conceptual introduction to correlated data. https://leanpub.com/correlateddata.

Rafferty, N. E., and A. R. Ives. 2013. Phylogenetic trait-based analyses of ecological networks. Ecology 94:2321-2333.

Simpson, Daniel, et al. 2017. Penalising model component complexity: A principled, practical approach to constructing priors. Statistical science 32(1): 1-28.

Li, D., Ives, A. R., & Waller, D. M. 2017. Can functional traits account for phylogenetic signal in community composition? New Phytologist, 214(2), 607-618.

Author

Anthony R. Ives, Daijiang Li, Russell Dinnage

Examples

## Structure of examples:
# First, a (brief) description of model types, and how they are specified
# - these are *not* to be run 'as-is'; they show how models should be organised
# Second, a run-through of how to simulate, and then analyse, data
# - these *are* to be run 'as-is'; they show how to format and work with data

# \donttest{
#############################################
### Brief summary of models and their use ###
#############################################
## Model structures from Ives & Helmus (2011)
if (FALSE) {
  # dat = data set for regression (note: must have a column "sp" and a column "site")
  # phy = phylogeny of class "phylo"
  # repulsion = to test phylogenetic repulsion or not

  # Model 1 (Eq. 1)
  z <- pglmm(freq ~ sp + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site),
    data = dat, family = "binomial",
    cov_ranef = list(sp = phy), REML = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, s2.init = .1
  )

  # Model 2 (Eq. 2)
  z <- pglmm(freq ~ sp + X + (1 | site) + (X | sp__),
    data = dat, family = "binomial",
    cov_ranef = list(sp = phy), REML = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, s2.init = .1
  )

  # Model 3 (Eq. 3)
  z <- pglmm(freq ~ sp * X + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site),
    data = dat, family = "binomial",
    cov_ranef = list(sp = phy), REML = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, s2.init = .1
  )

  ## Model structure from Rafferty & Ives (2013) (Eq. 3)
  # dat = data set
  # phyPol = phylogeny for pollinators (pol)
  # phyPlt = phylogeny for plants (plt)

  z <- pglmm(
    freq ~ pol * X + (1 | pol__) + (1 | plt__) + (1 | pol__@plt) +
      (1 | pol@plt__) + (1 | pol__@plt__),
    data = dat, family = "binomial",
    cov_ranef = list(pol = phyPol, plt = phyPlt),
    REML = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, s2.init = .1
  )
}

#####################################################
### Detailed analysis showing covariance matrices ###
#####################################################

# This is the example from section 4.3 in Ives, A. R. (2018) Mixed
# and phylogenetic models: a conceptual introduction to correlated data.

library(ape)

# Investigating covariance matrices for different types of model structure
nspp <- 6
nsite <- 4

# Simulate a phylogeny that has a lot of phylogenetic signal (power = 1.3)
phy <- compute.brlen(rtree(n = nspp), method = "Grafen", power = 1.3)

# Simulate species means
sd.sp <- 1
mean.sp <- rTraitCont(phy, model = "BM", sigma = sd.sp^2)

# Replicate values of mean.sp over sites
Y.sp <- rep(mean.sp, times = nsite)

# Simulate site means
sd.site <- 1
mean.site <- rnorm(nsite, sd = sd.site)

# Replicate values of mean.site over sp
Y.site <- rep(mean.site, each = nspp)

# Compute a covariance matrix for phylogenetic attraction
sd.attract <- 1
Vphy <- vcv(phy)

# Standardize the phylogenetic covariance matrix to have determinant = 1.
# (For an explanation of this standardization, see subsection 4.3.1 in Ives (2018))
Vphy <- Vphy / (det(Vphy)^(1 / nspp))

# Construct the overall covariance matrix for phylogenetic attraction.
# (For an explanation of Kronecker products, see subsection 4.3.1 in the book)
V <- kronecker(diag(nrow = nsite, ncol = nsite), Vphy)
# (a draw from the multivariate normal distribution with covariance matrix
# sd.attract^2 * V, from its Cholesky decomposition)
Y.attract <- array(t(chol(sd.attract^2 * V)) %*% rnorm(nrow(V)))

# Simulate residual errors
sd.e <- 1
Y.e <- rnorm(nspp * nsite, sd = sd.e)

# Construct the dataset
d <- data.frame(
  sp = rep(phy$tip.label, times = nsite),
  site = rep(1:nsite, each = nspp)
)

# Simulate abundance data
d$Y <- Y.sp + Y.site + Y.attract + Y.e

# Analyze the model
pglmm(Y ~ 1 + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site), data = d, cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))
#> Linear mixed model fit by restricted maximum likelihood
#> 
#> Formula: Y ~ 1 + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site)
#> 
#> logLik    AIC    BIC 
#> -47.12 106.25 113.31 
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>             Variance Std.Dev
#> 1|sp          0.1487  0.3856
#> 1|sp__        0.0000  0.0000
#> 1|site        0.0000  0.0000
#> 1|sp__@site   1.7499  1.3228
#> residual      0.8657  0.9305
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>                Value Std.Error Zscore Pvalue
#> (Intercept) -0.17353   0.63569 -0.273 0.7849
#> 

# Display random effects: the function `pglmm_plot_ranef()` does what
# the name implies. You can set `show.image = TRUE` and `show.sim.image = TRUE`
# to see the matrices and simulations.
re <- pglmm_plot_ranef(Y ~ 1 + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site) + (1 | sp__@site),
  data = d,
  cov_ranef = list(sp = phy), show.image = FALSE,
  show.sim.image = FALSE
)

#################################################
### Example of a bipartite phylogenetic model ###
#################################################

# Investigating covariance matrices for different types of model structure
nspp <- 20
nsite <- 15

# Simulate a phylogeny that has a lot of phylogenetic signal (power = 1.3)
phy.sp <- compute.brlen(rtree(n = nspp), method = "Grafen", power = 1.3)
phy.site <- compute.brlen(rtree(n = nsite), method = "Grafen", power = 1.3)

# Simulate species means
mean.sp <- rTraitCont(phy.sp, model = "BM", sigma = 1)

# Replicate values of mean.sp over sites
Y.sp <- rep(mean.sp, times = nsite)

# Simulate site means
mean.site <- rTraitCont(phy.site, model = "BM", sigma = 1)

# Replicate values of mean.site over sp
Y.site <- rep(mean.site, each = nspp)

# Generate covariance matrix for phylogenetic attraction among species
sd.sp.attract <- 1
Vphy.sp <- vcv(phy.sp)
Vphy.sp <- Vphy.sp / (det(Vphy.sp)^(1 / nspp))
V.sp <- kronecker(diag(nrow = nsite, ncol = nsite), Vphy.sp)
Y.sp.attract <- array(t(chol(sd.sp.attract^2 * V.sp)) %*% rnorm(nrow(V.sp)))

# Generate covariance matrix for phylogenetic attraction among sites
sd.site.attract <- 1
Vphy.site <- vcv(phy.site)
Vphy.site <- Vphy.site/(det(Vphy.site)^(1/nsite))
V.site <- kronecker(Vphy.site, diag(nrow = nspp, ncol = nspp))
Y.site.attract <- array(t(chol(sd.site.attract^2 * V.site)) %*% rnorm(nrow(V.site)))

# Generate covariance matrix for phylogenetic attraction of species:site interaction
sd.sp.site.attract <- 1
V.sp.site <- kronecker(Vphy.site, Vphy.sp)
Y.sp.site.attract <- array(t(chol(sd.sp.site.attract^2 * V.sp.site)) %*% rnorm(nrow(V.sp.site)))

# Simulate residual error
sd.e <- 0.5
Y.e <- rnorm(nspp*nsite, sd = sd.e)

# Construct the dataset
d <- data.frame(sp = rep(phy.sp$tip.label, times = nsite),
                site = rep(phy.site$tip.label, each = nspp))

# Simulate abundance data
d$Y <- Y.sp + Y.site + Y.sp.attract + Y.site.attract + Y.sp.site.attract + Y.e

# Plot random effects covariance matrices and then add phylogenies
# Note that, if show.image and show.sim are not specified, pglmm_plot_ranef() shows
# the covariance matrices if nspp * nsite < 200 and shows simulations
# if nspp * nsite > 100
re <- pglmm_plot_ranef(Y ~ 1 + (1|sp__) + (1|site__) + (1|sp__@site) +
                    (1|sp@site__) + (1|sp__@site__),
                    data=d, cov_ranef = list(sp = phy.sp, site = phy.site))


# This flips the phylogeny to match to covariance matrices
rot.phy.site <- phy.site
for(i in (nsite+1):(nsite+Nnode(phy.site)))
   rot.phy.site <- rotate(rot.phy.site, node = i)

plot(phy.sp, main = "Species", direction = "upward")

plot(rot.phy.site, main = "Site")


# Analyze the simulated data and compute a P-value for the (1|sp__@site__)
# random effect using a LRT. It is often better to fit the reduced model before
# the full model, because it s numerically easier to fit the reduced model,
# and then the parameter estimates from the reduced model can be given to the
# full model. In this case, I have used the estimates of the random effects
# from the reduce model, mod.r$ss, as the initial estimates for the same
# parameters in the full model in the statement s2.init=c(mod.r$ss, 0.01)^2.
# The final 0.01 is for the last random effect in the full model, (1|sp__@site__).
# Note also that the output of the random effects from communityPGLMM(), mod.r$ss,
# are the standard deviations, so they have to be squared for use as initial
# values of variances in mod.f.

mod.r <- pglmm(Y ~ 1 + (1|sp__) + (1|site__) + (1|sp__@site) + (1|sp@site__),
                        data = d, cov_ranef = list(sp = phy.sp, site = phy.site))
mod.f <- pglmm(Y ~ 1 + (1|sp__) + (1|site__) + (1|sp__@site) + (1|sp@site__) +
               (1|sp__@site__), data = d,
               cov_ranef = list(sp = phy.sp, site = phy.site),
               s2.init = c(mod.r$ss, 0.01)^2)
mod.f
#> Linear mixed model fit by restricted maximum likelihood
#> 
#> Formula: Y ~ 1 + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site__) + (1 | sp__@site) + (1 | sp@site__) + (1 | sp__@site__)
#> 
#> logLik    AIC    BIC 
#> -724.6 1467.3 1500.6 
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>                Variance   Std.Dev
